title: So how high is high enough?

cues.text: If waiting is worth money, why does she ever build at all? Why not wait for ever?
Because waiting is not free. Every month she waits, she gives up a month of profit she could have been making.
So there is some level of money coming in that is high enough that waiting any longer stops being worth it. That level has a name.
The trigger. The level the money coming in must reach before building is actually the right thing to do.
Here is Marshall's line again, where we left it.
Marshall's line stays exactly where it is. It is not wrong about arithmetic. But the line where Nell should actually build slides up above it.
And that gap has a meaning. It is the value of the chance to wait — the thing she destroys the moment she builds.
Build now, and the chance to wait is gone for ever. She has to be paid for that, and the gap is the price.
There is a mirror image of this on the way down, and chapter ten builds it properly.
Marshall says: shut down when the money stops covering the day-to-day costs.
The right answer is lower. She should absorb real losses before she gives up — because giving up throws away the chance of things getting better.
a trigger: high enough to stop waiting
